title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
High school academics
A note on scale carried over from before: pseo.participant’s n = 10,352 reflects the same near-complete, mostly-benign PSEO tracking gap discussed earlier — not a new concern.
Several variables show dramatically weaker effects here than against disconnected.cat — and in a few cases, the direction actually reverses. This is the richest set of divergences found yet in this comparison.
ACT score’s crossover effect nearly disappears. Against the combined measure, ACT score showed a strong, clean effect (eta² ≈ 1.9%, Persistently disconnected significantly higher than every other group). Here, the overall effect shrinks by nearly 90% (eta² ≈ 0.21%), and only one contrast survives (Persistently vs. Intermittently non-sustained, +0.621, p = .003) — the clean, complete ordering found against the combined measure is gone. This strongly confirms the hypothesis raised earlier: ACT score’s relationship with overall disconnection is mostly a no-record story, not an instability story — something to verify directly once we reach no_record.cat.
Took-ACT and PSEO participation both flip from protective to flat-or-reversed. Against disconnected.cat, both showed real protective effects (took.ACT: 7.5-point gap favoring test-takers; PSEO: 3.4-point gap favoring participants). Here: took.ACT shows almost no gap in Persistently non-sustained (16.0% vs. 15.5%) and, more tellingly, test-takers show a lower “Never non-sustained” rate (27.4% vs. 31.5%) — the opposite of protective. PSEO shows a similar reversal: Persistently non-sustained is actually higher for participants (17.2% vs. 15.6%). Both of these variables’ protective effects against overall disconnection appear to run almost entirely through avoiding no-record status, not through avoiding instability — a second and third confirmation of the same pattern found for ACT score.
CTE shows a genuinely more complex, non-monotonic story here than the clean gradient found against the combined measure. cte.achievement’s effect shrinks (V = 0.039 vs. 0.069) and its shape changes: at the “Persistently non-sustained” end, the expected protective gradient holds (CTE Concentrator/Completer 13.9% < Participant 15.8% < No CTE 16.8%), but at “Intermittently non-sustained,” the direction reverses — CTE Concentrators/Completers show the highest intermittent rate (43.2%), not the lowest. total.cte.courses.taken confirms this isn’t noise: Intermittently non-sustained shows significantly more CTE courses than every other category, including Never non-sustained. This suggests CTE engagement protects specifically against severe/persistent instability, while plausibly contributing to brief, intermittent instability — possibly reflecting the short-term employment transitions inherent to CTE work-based-learning placements (internships, apprenticeship-style courses ending and restarting).
AP exam is the one variable that holds up nearly unchanged. Persistently non-sustained: 20.7% (AP) vs. 15.4% (non-AP), V = 0.042 — comparable in both direction and magnitude to its effect against the combined measure (V = 0.051). AP exam appears to be a genuine instability-specific predictor, not one whose effect runs through no-record status.
MCA scores show a genuine subject-specific divergence: Science is now significant, Math and Reading are not. This is the reverse of the pattern found against disconnected.cat, where Math and Reading (weakly) reached significance and Science barely did. Here, MCA Science shows a clean, real effect (eta² ≈ 0.19%, p < .001): “Never non-sustained” scores significantly higher than all three other categories, which aren’t distinguished from each other — any instability at all associates with lower Science scores, not a dose-response pattern. Math (p = .069) and Reading (p = .230) are both non-significant here.
Overall Interpretation
This is the most revealing comparison yet between the combined and separated measures. Three variables that looked like broad protective factors against overall disconnection — ACT score’s crossover, ACT participation, and PSEO participation — turn out to have little or nothing to do with employment instability specifically; their apparent effect on disconnected.cat is almost certainly concentrated in no-record status instead, a hypothesis the upcoming no_record.cat analysis can confirm directly. AP exam is the one accomplishment variable that clearly does predict instability on its own terms. CTE reveals a genuinely more nuanced mechanism than the clean story from the combined measure suggested: it protects against the most severe instability while being associated with more frequent brief/intermittent instability, a distinction the combined measure’s monotonic gradient had completely flattened. MCA Science, not Math or Reading, is the academic-achievement measure that actually matters for instability specifically — the opposite of what mattered for overall disconnection.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Post-secondary
This is the single largest divergence found in this entire comparison, and it confirms the emerging pattern across nearly every other variable in this table. Against disconnected.cat, attended.ps was by far the dominant predictor (V = 0.195, nearly triple the next-strongest variable). Here, its effect drops to V = 0.077 — less than 40% of its original size, and no longer anywhere near the strongest predictor in the table (now comparable to Economic status and Gender, both around 0.08).
The most telling detail: “Never non-sustained” shows almost no gap at all between attendees and non-attendees (30.2% vs. 29.7%). Compare this to the combined measure, where “Consistently attached” showed attendees at roughly double the rate of non-attendees (17.4% vs. 8.6%). This means attempting postsecondary does essentially nothing to prevent instability from occurring at all — the massive protective effect seen against overall disconnection must be running almost entirely through avoiding no-record status, not through avoiding unstable employment. This is now the fourth variable (after ACT score, ACT participation, and PSEO) to show this same pattern, making it look less like a series of individual coincidences and more like a structural feature of this population: no-record status, not instability, is where most of these “protective” variables’ real effect lives.
Where attendance does matter here is in preventing instability from becoming chronic, not in preventing it altogether — the same reallocation pattern found for CTE. Attendees show a notably higher Intermittently non-sustained rate (43.6% vs. 37.6%) but a notably lower Persistently non-sustained rate (12.8% vs. 17.4%) and a modestly lower Broadly non-sustained rate (13.4% vs. 15.3%). In other words: attendees are just as likely to experience some instability as non-attendees, but when they do, it tends to resolve rather than persist — echoing exactly the pattern found for CTE achievement and total CTE courses.
Overall Interpretation
attended.ps’s enormous effect on overall disconnection turns out to be concentrated almost entirely in the no-record mechanism, not instability — attendees are no more likely to avoid unstable employment altogether than non-attendees, but they are considerably more likely to have that instability resolve rather than become chronic, and (presumably, pending the no_record.cat results) considerably less likely to disappear from the tracked system entirely. This is a genuinely important refinement of what was, until now, the single strongest finding in this whole disconnection analysis: attempting college doesn’t buy someone stability from day one, it appears to buy them resilience against instability turning permanent, and — more importantly — protection against falling out of the system altogether.

The Story This Data Tells
This comparison against disconnected.cat produced the clearest confirmation yet that overall disconnection persistence was hiding two genuinely different mechanisms. Four separate variables — ACT composite score, ACT participation, PSEO participation, and (most dramatically) attempting postsecondary at all — showed dramatically weaker, flat, or even reversed relationships with instability specifically, despite being among the strongest predictors of overall disconnection. This isn’t a coincidence repeated four times; it’s a structural pattern. These variables’ apparent protective power against disconnection overall is running almost entirely through avoiding no-record status, not through avoiding unstable employment — a hypothesis the no_record.cat analysis will now be able to test directly and, most likely, confirm.
The two demographic variables that mattered most for overall disconnection barely matter here, and vice versa. Special Ed status and English learner status — the two strongest predictors of disconnected.cat — collapse to two of the weakest predictors of instability specifically. Economic status and Gender, comparatively modest against the combined measure, become the strongest predictors here, with Gender’s effect size nearly doubling. This is a clean reallocation: whatever drives Special Ed and English learner students toward overall disconnection isn’t instability; whatever drives economically disadvantaged and female graduates toward disconnection largely is.
Race/Ethnicity’s most striking finding is a reversal for Asian/PI graduates specifically. Despite showing one of the highest persistent-disconnection rates overall, Asian/PI graduates show the lowest rate of persistent instability and the highest rate of avoiding instability altogether — meaning their overall disconnection story is almost certainly a no-record story, not an instability one. Black graduates show the opposite: a genuine, instability-specific disadvantage not fully visible in the combined measure.
A second, more subtle pattern emerged specifically for CTE-related variables and postsecondary attendance: they don’t prevent instability from happening, they prevent it from becoming chronic. Both CTE achievement/course count and attended.ps show a genuine reallocation from “persistent” toward “intermittent” instability, rather than a clean reduction in instability overall. This is a real, substantively interesting nuance the combined measure’s clean monotonic story didn’t reveal.
High school geographic and economic context shows no relationship with instability whatsoever — all three variables (Dem_Desc, local wages, local unemployment) are non-significant, continuing the pattern already found against the combined measure and strengthening the case that local context, if it matters at all in this framework, matters for the no-record mechanism specifically.
MCA subjects flip which one matters. Against the combined measure, Math and Reading were (weakly) significant and Science was borderline; here, only Science is significant, and Math/Reading are not. This is a genuine, if modest, divergence worth noting but not over-interpreting given how small all three effects are.
What This Sets Up
Nearly every major finding in this table points toward the same next step: no_record.cat should show the mirror image of what’s missing here. Specifically watch for: ACT score, ACT participation, PSEO, and attended.ps all showing much larger effects against no-record status than they did here; Special Ed and English learner status re-emerging as strong predictors; and local economic/geographic context finally showing a real relationship, if it’s going to show one anywhere. If that pattern holds, it will confirm that disconnected.cat’s “persistent disconnection” majority was really two distinct populations all along — one defined by chronic instability (driven by economic status, gender, AP exam, and to some extent CTE/attendance patterns), and one defined by disappearing from the tracked system entirely (driven by demographic and academic-achievement/college-engagement variables).

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Demographic variables
This table confirms almost every hypothesis raised by the non_sustained.cat comparison, variable for variable.
Special Ed status and English learner status re-emerge as strong predictors, nearly matching their strength against the combined measure. Special Ed: V = 0.087 here vs. 0.045 against non_sustained.cat — essentially a full reversal of where its effect lives. Persistently no-record: 25.6% (Special Ed) vs. 19.9% (others), and Never no-record: 43.7% vs. 53.4% — a genuine, substantial gap. English learner status shows the same pattern even more sharply: V = 0.105 here (identical to its effect against the combined measure) vs. 0.033 against instability. Persistently no-record: 35.2% (English learners) vs. 20.2% (others) — nearly double, and Never no-record: just 36.4% vs. 52.2%. This confirms directly what the instability analysis only implied: Special Ed and English learner students’ overall disconnection is almost entirely a no-record phenomenon, not an instability one.
Gender flips to essentially the weakest demographic predictor here, exactly as predicted. V = 0.025 (barely significant, p = .021), compared to V = 0.079 against instability. The gap in Persistently no-record is small (22.2% male vs. 20.1% female) and modest in every category. Gender’s relationship with workforce outcomes lives almost entirely in the instability mechanism, not disconnection from the record.
Economic status shows a similar, if less extreme, reversal. V = 0.050 here vs. 0.083 against instability — roughly the mirror image of Gender’s pattern. Economic disadvantage still shows a real gap (Persistently no-record: 20.2% vs. 22.4%, though in this table disadvantage actually shows a slightly lower no-record rate, worth noting as a genuine, if small, reversal in direction, not just magnitude) — economic status’s disconnection story is predominantly about instability, only weakly about disappearing from the record.
Race/Ethnicity reveals the sharpest and most important individual-group finding in this entire analysis: Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates show the two highest persistent no-record rates of any group, by a wide margin. Hispanic: 41.2% persistently no-record — the highest of any group. Asian/PI: 40.5% — nearly identical, and both roughly double White’s rate (20.6%). This is a dramatic confirmation of the hypothesis raised in the instability analysis: Asian/PI graduates showed the lowest persistent instability rate of any group, yet were among the highest overall-disconnection groups — this table shows exactly where that disconnection lives. Black graduates show a more moderate elevation (27.2%), while American Indian graduates are nearly identical to White (20.3% vs. 20.6%) — a genuine divergence from the instability table, where AI graduates showed the highest persistent instability rate of any group. Put together: AI graduates’ disadvantage is an instability story; Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates’ disadvantage is overwhelmingly a no-record story; Black graduates show a real, if more moderate, elevation in both.
Overall Interpretation
This table delivers exactly the confirmation the separated analysis was built to find. Every demographic variable that looked weak against instability (Special Ed, English learner) is strong here, and every variable that looked strong against instability (Gender, Economic status) is comparatively weak here — a clean, near-total reallocation of effect across the two mechanisms. The Race/Ethnicity findings are the most substantively important: this data shows that different racial/ethnic groups experience genuinely different forms of workforce disconnection, not just different overall rates — American Indian graduates’ disadvantage is concentrated in unstable-but-present employment, while Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates’ disadvantage is concentrated in disappearing from Minnesota’s tracked employment system entirely. This is a meaningfully more precise and more actionable finding than the combined measure could offer, and it argues for tailoring outreach or intervention strategies differently across these groups rather than treating “workforce disconnection” as a single, uniform experience.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
High school characteristics
Contrary to the hypothesis raised after the non_sustained.cat results, local economic context still does not show a strong or consistent relationship here — this needs to be stated plainly rather than reframed to fit expectations.
Average local wages remains completely non-significant (F(3,15165) = 0.67, p = .573, eta² ≈ 0.01%) — the third and final null result for this variable across all three dependent variables in this analysis. Local wage levels appear to have no bearing on any form of disconnection examined in this entire project’s non-completer analysis.
Average local unemployment rate does reach significance here, but the pattern is small and doesn’t fit a simple story. F(3,15165) = 6.21, p < .001, though eta² is still tiny (≈0.12%). The Tukey contrasts show something genuinely counterintuitive: Persistently no-record shows a significantly lower average local unemployment rate than both Intermittently no-record (−0.137, p < .001) and Broadly no-record (−0.123, p = .044) — the opposite of what you’d expect if a weak local labor market were pushing people out of the tracked system entirely. Intermittently no-record shows the highest rate, modestly above Never no-record (+0.075, p = .040). This is not a clean dose-response relationship, and given how small the effect size is, I’d be cautious about building a narrative around it rather than treating it as a genuine, well-supported pattern.
Dem_Desc reaches significance but remains one of the weakest effects found anywhere in this analysis (V = 0.021, p = .038, barely below the .05 threshold). The direction is consistent with the combined measure: Persistently no-record rises modestly with urbanicity (18.8% Entirely rural → 21.4% Town/rural mix → 21.5% Urban/town/rural mix), a small gradient in the same direction found against disconnected.cat.
Overall Interpretation
The hypothesis that local economic and geographic context would finally show a real relationship here — given that wages and unemployment mattered substantially for where sustained employment happened in the earlier point-in-time analysis — does not hold up. Local wages remain flatly irrelevant across all three disconnection measures, and while local unemployment rate does reach statistical significance here, the effect is tiny and the direction (persistent no-record status associated with lower, not higher, local unemployment) runs counter to a simple “weak local economy pushes people out of the system” story. This is worth reporting honestly as a negative or inconclusive finding rather than forcing an explanation: high school geographic and economic context, across all three framings of disconnection examined in this analysis, is simply not where the meaningful predictive signal lives for this population. Whatever drives long-term workforce disconnection for non-college graduates in Northeast Minnesota, it is not primarily rooted in the local labor market conditions of the high school they attended.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
High school academics
This table delivers the clearest, most complete confirmation yet of the hypotheses built up across this entire comparison — nearly every variable’s “true home” is now visible.
Took ACT (participation) shows its strongest effect of any table in this entire analysis, confirming it is almost entirely a no-record phenomenon. V = 0.098 here — actually larger than its effect against the combined measure (V = 0.075) and dramatically larger than against instability (V = 0.045, where the direction had even reversed). Persistently no-record: 16.8% (test-takers) vs. 24.2% (non-test-takers) — a 7.4-point gap. Never no-record: 56.3% vs. 47.6%. The earlier finding that ACT participation showed a flat-or-reversed relationship with instability, combined with this result, confirms conclusively: ACT participation protects against disappearing from the tracked system, and has essentially nothing to do with avoiding unstable employment.
PSEO participation shows the same pattern, and even more starkly than took.ACT relative to its own combined-measure effect. V = 0.070 here vs. 0.034 against the combined measure and a reversed, adverse direction against instability. Persistently no-record: 16.9% (PSEO) vs. 22.8% (non-PSEO) — a 5.9-point gap, nearly double what appeared in the combined measure. PSEO’s entire protective effect against overall disconnection lives here.
ACT composite score confirms the same story with a distinctive “threshold” shape. eta² ≈ 1.50% here (vs. 1.87% against the combined measure, vs. a mere 0.21% against instability) — nearly all of ACT score’s crossover effect is concentrated in no-record status. The shape is notable: Never no-record shows a significantly lower score than all three other categories (all three contrasts vs. Never are significant, roughly +0.93 to +1.33), but Intermittently, Broadly, and Persistently no-record are not distinguished from each other. This is a threshold effect, not a dose-response — any amount of no-record experience associates with a meaningfully higher ACT score among test-takers, but more years of it doesn’t compound the gap further.
CTE (both achievement and course count) shows a real, substantial effect here, comparable in strength to the combined measure and clearly stronger than its effect on instability. cte.achievement: V = 0.058 (vs. 0.069 combined, 0.039 instability), with Persistently no-record showing a clean gradient — CTE Concentrator/Completer (18.1%) < Participant (19.0%) < No CTE (25.0%), a 6.9-point spread, the widest specific gap in this table. total.cte.courses.taken confirms this: eta² ≈ 0.66%, with a real, largely monotonic protective pattern (Persistently no-record shows significantly fewer courses than every other category). This differs from the instability findings, where CTE showed a non-monotonic, reallocation pattern rather than a clean reduction — CTE’s protective effect is concentrated more in preventing disappearance from the record than in preventing chronic instability.
AP exam shows its weakest effect of any table so far, and a genuinely different shape. V = 0.030 (vs. 0.051 combined, 0.042 instability) — AP exam’s effect is actually more balanced between the two mechanisms than most other variables, tilting slightly toward instability rather than no-record. Notably, Persistently no-record is nearly identical between AP-takers and non-takers (21.3% vs. 21.3%) — AP’s effect here is concentrated entirely in the “Never” and “Intermittently” categories, not at the severe end.
MCA subjects show small, largely consistent effects across all three, similar in size to what was found against the combined measure — all three reach significance (eta² ≈ 0.09-0.11%), with Math and Reading showing the expected direction (lower scores among no-record groups) and Science showing, curiously, the opposite direction for the Persistently no-record contrast specifically (+0.081, p = .005) — a small, likely not very meaningful reversal given Science’s well-established missingness problems in this project, worth noting but not over-interpreting.
Overall Interpretation
This table completes the picture the entire non_sustained.cat/no_record.cat comparison was designed to reveal. ACT participation, PSEO participation, and (from the earlier table) attempting postsecondary at all are now confirmed as variables whose apparent “broad protective” effect against overall disconnection is almost entirely a no-record story — none of them meaningfully reduce instability, but all three substantially reduce the risk of disappearing from Minnesota’s tracked employment system. CTE shows a more genuinely dual-mechanism effect: real in both, but somewhat stronger here. AP exam is the interesting exception — its effect is the most evenly split of any accomplishment variable, and notably weaker here than elsewhere, suggesting it isn’t primarily a no-record-driving factor either, but a somewhat diffuse predictor of both mild instability and mild no-record risk without much force behind either.

text:
Post-secondary
As predicted, this is the largest effect found against no_record.cat — though the story is “primarily no-record,” not “exclusively no-record” as with ACT and PSEO. V = 0.148 here, compared to V = 0.077 against instability and V = 0.195 against the combined measure. This confirms attended.ps’s effect is concentrated in the no-record mechanism (roughly double the strength of its instability effect), but unlike ACT participation or PSEO — where the instability effect nearly vanished or reversed entirely — attended.ps retained a real, if smaller, protective effect on instability too (recall: Persistently non-sustained was 12.8% for attendees vs. 17.4% for non-attendees). This makes attended.ps the one variable in this entire analysis that shows a genuinely dual-mechanism effect rather than one that collapses almost entirely into a single pathway.
The gap here is the largest specific percentage-point gap found for this variable against either separated measure. Persistently no-record: 15.1% (attended) vs. 25.1% (never attended) — a 10-point gap. Never no-record: 59.8% vs. 45.6% — attendees are roughly 1.3x as likely to never disappear from the tracked system at all.
Overall Interpretation
This closes out the picture for attended.ps: attempting postsecondary education, even without completing it, delivers its largest protective benefit against disappearing from Minnesota’s tracked employment system entirely, but it also provides a real, smaller protective benefit against chronic instability — the only high-school/postsecondary-accomplishment variable examined in this entire analysis to show meaningful, non-trivial effects on both mechanisms simultaneously rather than concentrating almost entirely in one. This reinforces attended.ps’s standing as the single most important variable in this whole disconnection analysis: not just because its effect size is the largest, but because it’s the one variable whose benefit doesn’t have a major blind spot on either side of the non-sustained/no-record divide.

section: Summary: Bivariate Predictors of No-Record Persistence (no_record.cat)
text:
Summary: Bivariate Predictors of No-Record Persistence (no_record.cat)








Variable
Effect size
Direction




Attended postsecondary (attempt only)
V = 0.148
Strongest single predictor; attendance protects


English learner status
V = 0.105
EL → much more likely persistently no-record


Took ACT (participation)
V = 0.098
Participation → strongly protective


Special Ed status
V = 0.087
SpecialEd → more persistently no-record


ACT composite score (test-takers)
eta² ≈ 1.50%
Threshold effect — any no-record experience → higher score


PSEO participation
V = 0.070
PSEO → strongly protective


Race/Ethnicity
V = 0.060
Hispanic & Asian/PI → dramatically elevated


CTE achievement (categorical)
V = 0.058
More CTE → less no-record


Economic status
V = 0.050
Disadvantage → modestly more no-record


Total CTE courses (continuous)
eta² ≈ 0.66%
More courses → less no-record


AP exam participation
V = 0.030
Weak; balanced across both mechanisms


Gender
V = 0.025
Weak, barely significant


Dem_Desc
V = 0.021
Weakest significant effect; barely significant


MCA Math / Science
eta² ≈ 0.11% each
Negligible


MCA Reading
eta² ≈ 0.09%
Negligible


Average local unemployment rate
eta² ≈ 0.12%
Significant but tiny, non-monotonic, counterintuitive direction


Average local wages
Not significant (p = .573)
—



The Story This Data Tells
This table resolves nearly every open question raised by the non_sustained.cat comparison — it is the mirror image, almost variable for variable, of what was missing there. Four variables that showed dramatically weakened, flat, or reversed effects against instability — ACT composite score, ACT participation, PSEO participation, and attended.ps — all re-emerge here as among the strongest predictors in the entire analysis. This confirms, rather than just suggests, that overall disconnection persistence was masking two genuinely separate populations: one whose disadvantage is rooted in unstable-but-present employment, and one whose disadvantage is rooted in disappearing from Minnesota’s tracked employment system altogether. Most of the variables long assumed to be broadly “protective” for non-completers turn out to protect against only one of these two things, not both.
Attempting postsecondary education remains the single most important variable in this entire analysis, and it’s now clear why it dominated the combined measure. Its effect here (V = 0.148) is nearly double its effect against instability (V = 0.077) — but unlike ACT and PSEO, it didn’t collapse to near-zero on the instability side. attended.ps is the one variable in this whole analysis that delivers a genuine, non-trivial benefit on both mechanisms simultaneously, which is exactly why it towered over every other predictor in the combined disconnected.cat measure.
Special Education and English learner status — the two strongest predictors of overall disconnection — are confirmed here as being almost entirely no-record phenomena. Both variables, which nearly vanished against instability, come roaring back here at effect sizes matching or exceeding their combined-measure strength. Whatever barriers these two groups face in the workforce, they manifest overwhelmingly as absence from the tracked system, not as cycling through unstable jobs.
Race/Ethnicity produces the most substantively important and actionable finding across this entire three-part analysis. Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates show persistent no-record rates around double White graduates’ rate — the widest individual-group gap found anywhere in this project — while American Indian graduates, who showed the highest persistent instability rate of any group, look no different from White graduates here. This means three different racial/ethnic groups are experiencing three genuinely different forms of disadvantage: AI graduates face an instability problem, Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates face a disconnection-from-the-system problem, and Black graduates show a real, more moderate elevation on both.
High school geographic and economic context is confirmed, across all three dependent variables, to be essentially irrelevant to this population’s workforce disconnection. Average local wages is non-significant everywhere; average local unemployment rate reaches statistical significance only here, but the effect is tiny and runs in a counterintuitive direction (persistent no-record status associated with lower, not higher, local unemployment) that shouldn’t be over-interpreted. Whatever drives long-term disconnection for this population, it is not rooted in the economic conditions of the high school district they came from.
What This Sets Up
Taken together, the three-part comparison (disconnected.cat, non_sustained.cat, no_record.cat) has produced a genuinely richer and more actionable picture than the original combined measure could have: (1) economic status and gender predict instability specifically; (2) Special Ed and English learner status, along with ACT/PSEO/postsecondary-attempt variables, predict no-record status specifically; (3) attended.ps and CTE are the two variables that meaningfully address both mechanisms; and (4) Race/Ethnicity reveals that different groups face genuinely different forms of disadvantage that a single combined outcome measure would have blurred together. This three-way comparison — not any single table — is the real deliverable of this bivariate stage, and it should directly shape how the multivariate confirmation models are structured: likely as two separate model sequences (mirroring the DV1a/DV1b-style split used earlier in this project), one for instability persistence and one for no-record persistence, rather than a single combined disconnection model.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Executive Summary
This analysis examined the 58% of Northeast Minnesota high school graduates who never completed a postsecondary credential, tracing their workforce participation across the first five years after exiting formal education. Three major findings anchor this work:

Disconnection is not a transitional phase — it is the majority experience. 53.2% of non-college graduates are persistently disconnected from sustained employment (4-5 of their first 5 years), and only 11.9% are consistently attached.
“Disconnection” is not one phenomenon — it is at least two, and they behave completely differently. Separating unstable-but-present employment (non-sustained work) from complete absence from Minnesota’s tracked system (no-record status) revealed that these two mechanisms have almost entirely different predictors, different trajectories over time, and different underlying stories.
Underutilization, not disengagement, is the dominant experience for those who aren’t stably employed — 73-81% of non-sustained employment involves at least partial regional attachment, meaning most instability reflects people working in the region, just not enough to be “sustained,” not people leaving for opportunity elsewhere.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
The Story This Data Tells

Part 1: The scale and shape of the problem
Picture the roughly 15,000 non-college graduates who make up this population. In their first year out, they’re widely dispersed — a little over a third in unstable work, roughly a fifth each in no-record status, still-attending-postsecondary, and sustained regional employment. But this snapshot obscures the real story: tracked over five years, this population sorts into a stark and durable pattern. Just over half end up persistently disconnected; barely one in eight ever achieve full, sustained attachment. Two very different trajectories are unfolding simultaneously — sustained employment does grow steadily every year (30.2% → 40.1% of the population from Year 1 to Year 5) — but “no Minnesota employment record” grows even faster, overtaking every other category by Year 5. Non-sustained employment, meanwhile, consistently shrinks — but critically, when we looked closely at where that non-sustained employment happens, we found the large majority (73-81%, holding steady across all five years) involves at least partial regional attachment. This is underutilization, not outmigration: most people who aren’t stably employed are still here, working, just not enough.


Part 2: Two distinct disconnection mechanisms hiding inside one number
The single most important methodological move in this analysis was splitting “disconnected” into its two components — non-sustained employment and no employment record at all — and testing each independently. This wasn’t a formality; it fundamentally changed the picture:

The two measures have genuinely different shapes. Non-sustained persistence is front-loaded toward the intermittent middle (39.8% of the population) and shrinks steadily — a phenomenon that resolves over time. No-record persistence is bimodal (51.0% never, 21.3% persistent) and, once someone crosses into the “broad” category, they’re far more likely to escalate into “persistent” than to plateau — a phenomenon that compounds.
Decomposing the “persistently disconnected” majority revealed three roughly equal populations, not one. 40.1% of the persistently disconnected got there mainly through no-record status, 29.5% mainly through instability, and 30.4% through a genuine, chronic alternation between both that neither individual measure alone would have identified.
Nearly every bivariate predictor split cleanly onto one side of this divide or the other, and in several cases the split was total.



Part 3: Which characteristics drive which mechanism
Demographics split almost perfectly across the two mechanisms. Special Education status and English learner status — the two strongest predictors of overall disconnection — turned out to be driven almost entirely by no-record status; both showed weak, sometimes reversed relationships with instability. Economic status and Gender showed the opposite pattern: comparatively modest against the combined measure, but the strongest demographic predictors of instability specifically, with Gender’s effect size nearly doubling once isolated.
Race/Ethnicity revealed the most consequential and actionable divergence in the whole analysis. Three different racial/ethnic groups face three different forms of disadvantage: American Indian graduates show the highest persistent-instability rate of any group but look no different from White graduates on no-record status; Hispanic and Asian/PI graduates show the opposite — roughly double the persistent no-record rate of White graduates, but Asian/PI graduates actually show the lowest persistent-instability rate of any group; Black graduates show a real, more moderate elevation on both. Treating “disconnection” as one undifferentiated outcome would have completely obscured these three distinct patterns.
High school accomplishments split into three groups of variables, not two. ACT participation, PSEO participation, and ACT composite score all turned out to be almost purely no-record predictors — their apparent broad protective effect against overall disconnection nearly vanished or reversed once instability was isolated. AP exam participation was the reverse case — a real instability predictor with almost no no-record effect. CTE engagement and, most importantly, attempting postsecondary education at all were the two variables that showed genuine, meaningful effects on both mechanisms — attended.ps in particular remained the single strongest predictor in this entire analysis precisely because it’s the only variable that doesn’t have a blind spot on either side of the divide.
High school geographic and economic context was, across all three framings of disconnection, essentially irrelevant. Local wages showed no relationship with any outcome examined. Local unemployment rate reached significance only against no-record status, but the effect was tiny and ran in a counterintuitive direction. Whatever drives long-term disconnection for this population, it is not rooted in the local economic conditions of the high school they attended — a genuine and somewhat surprising departure from what these same variables showed throughout the rest of this project’s college-completer analyses.


Part 4: A unifying picture
Put all of this together, and a clear structural story emerges. This population’s long-term workforce outcomes are shaped by two largely independent forces: whether someone ever engaged with the postsecondary system at all (attendance, ACT, PSEO) — which mainly determines whether they stay visible in Minnesota’s tracked employment system — and a separate set of demographic and programmatic factors (economic status, gender, CTE, AP) that mainly determine whether the employment they do have is stable. Geography and local economic conditions, so influential elsewhere in this project, play almost no role here. And underneath both mechanisms sits a genuine equity story: different demographic groups aren’t just disconnected at different rates, they’re disconnected in different ways — a distinction that matters enormously for what kind of intervention would actually help.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: What This Sets Up for the Multivariate Stage
text:
What This Sets Up for the Multivariate Stage
This bivariate work points toward a clear multivariate design, directly analogous to the DV1a/DV1b structure used earlier in this project’s college-completer analysis:

Two separate model sequences, not one combined model — one for non_sustained.cat persistence, one for no_record.cat persistence — since a single combined model would recreate the same masking problem this entire analysis was built to solve.
attended.ps belongs in both models as a foundational predictor, given it’s the only variable shown to matter for both mechanisms.
Expect substantial attenuation for Special Ed and English learner status once academic/accomplishment variables enter the no-record model — mirroring the exact pattern found throughout the rest of this project (e.g., the MCA-missingness masking effect discovered in the college-completer work).
Local geographic/economic variables can likely be deprioritized or dropped from both models given their consistent null results across all three outcome framings — though worth retaining at least once to formally confirm rather than assume.
Race/Ethnicity should be watched closely for interaction effects — given that AI, Hispanic/Asian-PI, and Black graduates show genuinely different mechanisms of disadvantage, a single additive coefficient per race category may not fully capture what’s happening, and this is worth flagging as a candidate for deeper stratified analysis (per the original methodology’s Step 3.3) even if it’s not built into the initial multivariate pass.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between location of postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(9) = 2713.62, Cramer’s V = 0.197, p < .001, N = 23,341【772†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 3699.62, Cramer’s V = 0.207, p < .001, N = 28,840【773†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 1609.04, Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001, N = 19,827【774†source】

The association is moderate in years 1 and 5 and slightly weaker by year 10. The central divide is that regional PS graduates are consistently more likely to work in the region, while graduates outside MN or at MN institutions outside the region are more likely to pursue statewide or out‑of‑state pathways.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Regional graduates show the strongest immediate tie to local jobs, with 65.8% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 23.8% of non‑graduates, 28.7% of MN graduates outside the region, and 22.0% of graduates outside MN. Non‑graduates are most often disconnected (43.4% “not meaningful” and 25.9% “no record”)【772†source】.
Year 5: Regional graduates remain highly concentrated in regional employment (50.2%), far above MN graduates outside the region (18.3%) or graduates outside MN (20.4%). By contrast, MN graduates outside the region have the highest statewide employment (44.0%), reflecting mobility within the state. Non‑graduates remain more disconnected (28.4% “not meaningful” and 31.0% “no record”)【773†source】.
Year 10: Regional graduates sustain a long‑term edge in local employment (43.1%), while MN graduates outside the region remain more mobile (38.0% in statewide employment). Graduates outside MN have lower regional (20.7%) and statewide (17.8%) employment, with a higher share of disconnection (49.4% “no record”). Non‑graduates remain the weakest group, with only 25.6% regional employment and the highest share of disconnection (36.7% “no record”)【774†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that regional PS graduation strongly anchors individuals in the local workforce, while graduation outside the region or outside MN promotes mobility and statewide attachment. Non‑graduates remain at the greatest risk of disconnection across all timeframes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Highest Credential Level (highest.cred.level)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between highest credential earned and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(20) = 25,119.08, Cramer’s V = 0.366, p < .001, N = 46,777【760†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(20) = 7,371.79, Cramer’s V = 0.231, p < .001, N = 34,683【761†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1,030.86, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 19,828【762†source】

The association is strong in the first year, moderates by year 5, and weakens further by year 10, though it remains significant. The key distinction is that higher credentials (Bachelor’s or above) delay regional employment but lead to stronger statewide employment later, while lower or mid‑level credentials (Associate, less than Associate) are more tied to early and sustained regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students with no college are most likely to be in regional meaningful employment (19.9%), but also heavily represented in disconnection categories (44.2% not meaningful, 30.1% no record). Those with some college or Associate degrees show moderate regional employment (18–19%) but are strongly concentrated in “attending PS” (49–69%). Students pursuing a Bachelor’s or higher overwhelmingly remain in education (86.5%) and show the lowest regional employment (5.7%)【760†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment peaks among less than Associate (42.3%) and Associate degree earners (36.5%), with some college also relatively strong (29.2%). By contrast, Bachelor’s or higher show lower regional attachment (19.1%) but higher statewide meaningful employment (20.5%). Non‑college individuals still show significant disconnection (27.4% not meaningful, 37.0% no record)【761†source】.
Year 10: The regional advantage of Associate and sub‑Associate credentials remains high (42–43%), while Bachelor’s or higher show stronger statewide employment (27.9%) and lower regional employment (26.5%). Non‑college individuals continue to show the weakest outcomes, with the highest disconnection rates (41.7% no record)【762†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that mid‑level credentials (Associate and below) strongly anchor individuals in regional employment, while Bachelor’s and above foster statewide mobility and stronger longer‑term outcomes, and no credential consistently yields the weakest employment stability.

Strongest Associations
- The attendance variables (attended within 1st year, ever attended) and postsecondary graduation have the strongest early associations, with Cramer’s V values above 0.5–0.6 at Year 1. These measures clearly separate students who pursue higher education from those who do not, with PS attenders/graduates far less likely to enter immediate regional work but more likely to gain stable employment outcomes over time.

Moderate Associations

Regional PS graduates are far more likely to remain in local employment, while graduates from 4‑year universities or from outside the region show greater statewide mobility.
Regional Employment Predictors
- Non‑attenders and non‑graduates are consistently more likely to enter regional meaningful employment early, but they also carry much higher risks of disconnection in the long run.

- Bachelor’s+ degrees, 4‑year universities, and graduation outside MN are consistently tied to statewide employment and mobility, reducing regional anchoring.
Overall Insight
Postsecondary experiences draw a clear line between regional anchoring vs. statewide mobility.
1. Access and completion of postsecondary education lead to broader statewide opportunities and reduced risk of disconnection.
2. Absence of postsecondary pathways results in earlier regional employment but higher long‑term vulnerability.
3. The type, level, and location of postsecondary attainment nuance this divide: regional and 2‑year pathways strengthen local attachment, while higher‑level and out‑of‑region pathways expand opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the sector of postsecondary graduation (4‑year public, 2‑year public, other) and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(12) = 1313.46, Cramer’s V = 0.138, p < .001, N = 22,962【748†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1181.64, Cramer’s V = 0.152, p < .001, N = 17,154【749†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 498.68, Cramer’s V = 0.160, p < .001, N = 9,691【750†source】

The relationship is moderate but consistent, strengthening slightly by year 10. The main divide is between 4‑year and 2‑year graduates, with different propensities toward statewide vs. regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Almost all graduates remain in postsecondary, but small differences emerge. 2‑year graduates show the highest early regional employment (20.6%), compared to 7.1% among “other” graduates and just 4.5% among 4‑year graduates. Graduates of 4‑year and “other” institutions overwhelmingly remain enrolled (86%+), delaying workforce entry【748†source】.
Year 5: Clearer differences appear. 2‑year graduates lead in regional meaningful employment (40.7%), while 4‑year graduates show higher statewide employment (21.8%). “Other” graduates also lean toward regional work (21.7%). Disconnection rates are somewhat higher among 4‑year graduates, but overall the trend is that 2‑year pathways support stronger early attachment to regional jobs【749†source】.
Year 10: By this point, differences remain. 2‑year graduates sustain the highest regional meaningful employment (45.1%), while 4‑year graduates lean toward statewide meaningful employment (29.5%). “Other” graduates remain in the middle with balanced outcomes. Importantly, no‑record rates are lowest for 2‑year graduates (21.6%), suggesting stronger regional retention. In contrast, 4‑year graduates have higher statewide outcomes but also higher “no record” rates (33.6%)【750†source】.
Overall, institution sector matters: 2‑year graduates show stronger long‑term regional employment, while 4‑year graduates pursue statewide opportunities and are more mobile, and “other” graduates fall between.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
AP Exam Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between AP exam participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 822.44, Cramer’s V = 0.133, p < .001, N = 46,777【581†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 301.32, Cramer’s V = 0.093, p < .001, N = 34,683【582†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 113.60, Cramer’s V = 0.076, p < .001, N = 19,828【583†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and declines over time, though remains statistically significant. The primary relationship is that AP exam participants are much more likely to attend postsecondary, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is substantially higher among non‑AP students (16.1% vs. 7.7%), while AP exam participants are much more likely to be in postsecondary (68.8% vs. 45.7%). Disconnection is lower for AP participants (6.7% vs. 12.2%)【581†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Non‑AP students retain an advantage in regional meaningful employment (27.4% vs. 17.1%), while AP participants show higher rates of statewide meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 14.7%) and continued postsecondary enrollment (23.7% vs. 15.3%). Disconnection rates are similar (~21%)【582†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains higher for non‑AP students (29.9% vs. 22.7%). AP participants hold an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (27.0% vs. 18.7%). Disconnection is slightly higher for AP participants (36.0% vs. 32.1%), suggesting some trade‑off in regional attachment over time【583†source】.
Overall, AP exam participation sorts students into pathways favoring education and statewide employment, while non‑participants maintain stronger ties to regional meaningful employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Reading (MCA.R)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Reading scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42500) = 689.45, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 31013) = 119.45, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 17590) = 237.15, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant over time. The primary pattern is that higher MCA Reading scores are associated with postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are more tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful/disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score about +0.26 higher than regional meaningful workers (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.09) and No MN record (+0.14) also score higher than regional meaningful (p ≤ .02).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is linked to lower reading scores, while higher scores track into postsecondary and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.21), statewide meaningful (+0.17), and No MN record (+0.08) all score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores slightly below regional meaningful (−0.17, p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment sits lower on the MCA-R spectrum, while postsecondary and statewide jobs skew higher.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.18) and No MN record (+0.14) are significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores considerably lower (−0.25, p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains tied to lower MCA-R scores, with higher scores concentrated in statewide meaningful employment or outside tracked records.
Overall, MCA Reading reinforces that academic achievement predicts longer-term educational and statewide work pathways, while lower scores are associated with stronger regional attachment but also greater risk of not meaningful outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Post-Secondary Enrollment Options (PSEO) Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between PSEO participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3076.21, Cramer’s V = 0.290, p < .001, N = 36,625【542†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 430.00, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 24,531【543†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 77.28, Cramer’s V = 0.089, p < .001, N = 9,676【544†source】

The strength of association is very strong in the first year but weakens considerably over time. The primary relationship is that PSEO participants are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment early on.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is higher among non‑PSEO students (18.4%) compared to PSEO participants (12.6%). In contrast, PSEO participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary (61.8% vs. 33.6%). Disconnection is notably lower among PSEO participants (6.5% vs. 16.2%)【542†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment gaps narrow (28.1% non‑PSEO vs. 25.1% PSEO). Importantly, PSEO participants surpass non‑participants in meaningful employment statewide (18.0% vs. 13.3%). Postsecondary attendance is higher among PSEO students (19.1% vs. 11.9%), while disconnection is lower (18.7% vs. 23.5%)【543†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is relatively similar (29.7% non‑PSEO vs. 26.8% PSEO). PSEO participants maintain higher statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 16.9%), while disconnection rates are similar (~32%). The long‑term pattern suggests PSEO participants transition from education into statewide meaningful jobs, while non‑participants retain an edge in regional meaningful employment【544†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
SAT Test Participation (SAT Taken)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the SAT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 228.74, Cramer’s V = 0.070, p < .001, N = 46,777【595†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 188.76, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 34,683【596†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 99.99, Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001, N = 19,828【597†source】

The effect sizes are small but consistent. The key pattern is that SAT takers are far more likely to attend postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: SAT takers are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (73.5% vs. 47.3% for non‑takers). Regional meaningful employment is much lower for SAT takers (3.2% vs. 15.5%), while disconnection is also somewhat lower (9.0% vs. 11.7%)【595†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: SAT takers maintain higher postsecondary enrollment (30.1% vs. 15.8%). Regional meaningful employment is still much lower (7.6% vs. 26.8%). Interestingly, SAT takers are slightly more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (18.2% vs. 15.1%). Disconnection is higher among SAT takers (28.6% vs. 20.9%)【596†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: SAT takers continue to show very low regional meaningful employment (11.5% vs. 29.5%), while statewide meaningful employment is similar (18.6% vs. 19.4%). Disconnection is much higher among SAT takers (55.9% vs. 32.0%)【597†source】.
Overall, SAT participation identifies a small group of students who overwhelmingly pursue postsecondary initially, but long‑term outcomes show weak regional attachment and much higher disconnection, suggesting that SAT takers may be more mobile, pursue opportunities outside the region or state, or leave tracked employment systems altogether.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Science (MCA.S)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Science scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 37501) = 544.02, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 26050) = 160.29, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 11879) = 81.74, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant through 10 years. The key pattern is that higher MCA Science scores are associated with postsecondary education and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score substantially higher than regional meaningful (+0.38, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful (+0.07) also scores higher than regional meaningful (p = .025).
- Not meaningful (−0.07) and No MN record (−0.12) score below postsecondary.
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful work is tied to lower MCA-S scores, while education and statewide jobs are tied to higher scores.
Year 5:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.25) and postsecondary (+0.32) are far above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record (+0.11) is also higher.
- Not meaningful (−0.04) is slightly below regional meaningful (p = .044).
- Takeaway: by 5 years, the gap widens, with statewide and postsecondary pathways clearly tied to higher MCA-S scores, while regional meaningful remains lower.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.27) and No MN record (+0.18) score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.31) scores well below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower MCA-S scores, while higher scores push students into statewide jobs or out of tracked MN employment.
Overall, MCA Science mirrors the MCA Reading pattern: academic achievement is strongly tied to educational and statewide pathways, while lower achievement is associated with stronger regional attachment or risk of weaker employment outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
CTE Achievement
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between CTE achievement (Concentrator/Completer, Participant, No CTE) and post‑graduation outcomes across all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 508.14, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 46,777【663†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 307.50, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 34,683【664†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 174.53, Cramer’s V = 0.066, p < .001, N = 19,828【665†source】

The associations are modest but consistent. The clearest relationship is that CTE Concentrators/Completers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while students with no CTE are more likely to be in postsecondary or outside regional attachment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for CTE Concentrators/Completers (19.4%), compared to Participants (15.1%) and No CTE students (12.6%). Postsecondary enrollment is much higher among No CTE (51.3%) and Participants (49.2%) than Concentrators/Completers (41.5%). This suggests that CTE pathways steer students more quickly into regional work while non‑CTE students delay employment through postsecondary【663†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: The regional employment gap persists: 31.9% for Concentrators/Completers vs. 27.2% for Participants and 22.9% for No CTE. Postsecondary attendance is relatively low across all groups (13–17%), but still higher for those without CTE. Concentrators/Completers maintain stronger local employment connections, while non‑CTE students lean slightly more toward statewide employment (15.7%)【664†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains strongest among Concentrators/Completers (34.6%), compared to Participants (29.1%) and No CTE students (25.5%). Statewide meaningful employment is more evenly distributed, while disconnection is highest among those with No CTE (35.5%). The long‑term pattern confirms that CTE achievement reinforces regional employment pathways, while students outside CTE are more likely to leave the region or experience disconnection【665†source】.
Overall, CTE achievement consistently predicts stronger regional workforce attachment, distinguishing Concentrators/Completers as the group most likely to remain engaged in meaningful employment within the region over time.

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
As we move from descriptive analysis to predictive modeling, the goal is to retain the strongest predictors while removing weaker or redundant ones.
Below is a structured list by section.



Keep / Prioritize
- SpecialEd Status (strongest demographic predictor)
- Race/Ethnicity (moderate strength, important equity covariate)
Drop / Deprioritize
- Gender (weak, V ≈ .05–.10, fades over time)
- English Learner (very weak, V < .07, small group sizes)
- Economic Status (moderate but weaker compared to later predictors; may retain as a control if needed)




Keep / Prioritize
- Dem_Desc (Rural/Urban) – moderate, useful contextual control
- Avg. Unemployment – strong early F-values, local context matters
- Avg. Wages % State – strong F-values, economic environment indicator
Drop / Deprioritize
- Range School (very weak effect, V ≈ .03–.05)




Keep / Prioritize
- ACT (took ACT, ACT Composite Score) – strong, differentiates pathways
- MCA (Math strongest, Reading & Science secondary) – critical academic predictors
- CTE Achievement – anchors to regional meaningful employment
- Total CTE Courses Taken – consistent predictor of regional attachment
- PSEO Participation – strong early differentiator of statewide vs regional pathways
Drop / Deprioritize
- SAT Taken (consistently weak, V ≈ .07, redundant with ACT)
- AP Exam (moderate, but less powerful than ACT/MCA; may be dropped if multicollinearity is high)




Keep / Prioritize
- Attended Postsecondary Within First Year – strongest early effect (V > .5)
- Ever Attended Postsecondary – very strong differentiator (V > .6)
- Postsecondary Graduation – critical predictor of long-term stability
- Highest Credential Level – strong differentiator between statewide vs regional pathways
- Graduation Location – strong anchor for regional vs statewide attachment
Drop / Deprioritize
- Institution Sector – moderate only (V ≈ .14–.16); may be redundant with credential level & location





Drop: Gender, English Learner, Range School, SAT Taken, possibly AP Exam, possibly Institution Sector

Keep: All others, with focus on SpecialEd, Race/Ethnicity, local economic indicators, ACT/MCA, CTE, and Postsecondary attendance/graduation/credentials.

This balances parsimony (leaner model) with coverage (keeping conceptually important drivers of outcomes).

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Unemployment Rate (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the county unemployment rate during high school and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on unemployment rate across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46772) = 12.55, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 13.03, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19745) = 9.69, p < .001

Effects are modest but reliable across years.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Attending postsecondary comes from higher‑unemployment counties than Meaningful employment in the region (Δ = +0.118, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also higher than Meaningful region (Δ ≈ +0.07 to +0.08, both p < .05).
- Takeaway: in the first year, regional meaningful employment is associated with comparatively lower local unemployment than several alternative pathways.
Year 5:
- Meaningful MN (statewide) > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.146, p < .001).
- Attending ps and No MN record are lower than Meaningful MN (Δ ≈ −0.091 and −0.088, both p ≤ .004).
- Takeaway: by five years out, statewide meaningful employment is associated with higher‑unemployment counties than regional meaningful jobs, while continued schooling and no record skew lower than statewide meaningful.
Year 10:
- Meaningful MN > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.088, p = .0009).
- Not meaningful > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.067, p = .022).
- No MN record < Meaningful MN and < Not meaningful (Δ = −0.103 and −0.082; p ≤ .002).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower unemployment contexts than statewide meaningful and not meaningful routes; those with no MN record tend to come from lower‑unemployment counties than peers in statewide/not‑meaningful outcomes.
Overall, the pattern suggests that students from lower‑unemployment counties are more likely to land in meaningful employment within the region, whereas higher‑unemployment origins are more often associated with statewide meaningful, not meaningful, or continued schooling pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Range School Context
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending a Range school and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 173.72, Cramer’s V = 0.061, p < .001, N = 46,777【487†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 63.68, Cramer’s V = 0.043, p < .001, N = 34,683【488†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 57.03, Cramer’s V = 0.054, p < .001, N = 19,828【489†source】

The strength of association is weak overall but consistent. The primary relationship is that Range school students are more likely to achieve meaningful employment in the region compared to non‑Range peers, though differences in postsecondary attendance and disconnection are modest.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is slightly higher among Range school students (16.6% vs. 15.0%). Range students are also somewhat more likely to be attending postsecondary (52.1% vs. 46.6%) and less likely to be in not meaningful work (17.8% vs. 21.8%). Disconnection is lower for Range students (10.2% vs. 12.1%)【487†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment advantages grow, with 29.3% of Range graduates employed in the region compared to 25.8% of non‑Range peers. Postsecondary enrollment remains somewhat higher (17.3% vs. 15.7%), while not meaningful and disconnection outcomes are slightly lower for Range graduates (19.6% vs. 21.7% and 19.3% vs. 21.5%)【488†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment becomes more pronounced: 34.0% of Range graduates vs. 28.0% of non‑Range graduates. Range graduates maintain comparable statewide meaningful employment (18.4% vs. 19.7%), and their disconnection remains modestly lower (29.7% vs. 33.1%)【489†source】. The long‑term trend indicates that Range school students are more attached to regional meaningful work than non‑Range peers.

title: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
This one-page overview integrates effect size tables, key insights, and a visual comparison chart across all four major sections of analysis.




Demographics
- Strongest predictor: SpecialEd Status (V = 0.258, Yr 1).
- Demographics fade in importance over time; SpecialEd and Race/Ethnicity remain the most relevant.
High School Characteristics
- Local economic conditions (unemployment, wages) significantly shape early outcomes (F = 53.1 for unemployment, Yr 1).
- Rural/urban divides also matter, but effects diminish by Year 10.
High School Accomplishments
- Academic/college-prep measures (ACT, MCA, PSEO, AP) → statewide pathways, less regional attachment.
- CTE achievement and course load → strongest predictors of regional meaningful employment.
- MCA Math has the largest overall predictive power (F = 1344.5, Yr 1).
Postsecondary Experiences
- The most powerful overall predictors.
- Attendance and graduation separate students into statewide vs. regional pathways.
- Credential level and location nuance outcomes: regional/2-year credentials anchor locally, 4-year/out-of-state expand mobility.







Effect Sizes Overview







Regional meaningful employment is most strongly tied to CTE in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.

Statewide employment and mobility stem from academic success and 4-year/out-of-state credentials.

Disconnection is concentrated among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker preparation, amplified by local economic stressors.

This highlights a dual pathway model:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → strong anchoring in the local workforce.
Both are vital in shaping Northeast Minnesota’s labor market outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Special Education Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between Special Education status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3110.70, Cramer’s V = 0.258, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 829.87, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 231.15, Cramer’s V = 0.108, p < .001, N = 19,828

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, but the relationship remains significant. The primary pattern is that SpecialEd students are less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. While regional meaningful employment is roughly equal at Year 1, by Years 5 and 10 non-SpecialEd students pull ahead in meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is nearly the same for SpecialEd (15.6%) and non-SpecialEd (15.3%). The sharpest differences are in education and disconnection: only 21.4% of SpecialEd students are attending postsecondary compared to 52.5% of non-SpecialEd, and 25.1% of SpecialEd students are disconnected compared to 9.3% of non-SpecialEd. This points to an early divergence where SpecialEd students are disproportionately outside of education and tracked employment.
5 Years After Graduation: Gaps in regional meaningful employment begin to open (SpecialEd 24.6% vs. non-SpecialEd 26.8%). SpecialEd students are still much less likely to be in postsecondary (6.8% vs. 17.6%) and more likely to be not meaningful (29.1% vs. 20.0%) or disconnected (30.0% vs. 19.5%). By this stage, non-SpecialEd students strengthen their advantage in both education and regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment widens further (SpecialEd 24.7% vs. non-SpecialEd 29.9%). Non-SpecialEd students are also more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (20.6% vs. 11.7%). SpecialEd students remain more concentrated in disconnected outcomes (36.9% vs. 31.7%). The long-term trajectory shows that SpecialEd students are less attached to meaningful regional work and face persistent disadvantages in education and quality employment.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Across all three variable groups — demographic characteristics, high school characteristics, and high school accomplishments — the factors most strongly associated with post-secondary attendance are individual-level characteristics, not school- or community-level ones.
Among demographic predictors, special education status and economic disadvantage stand out as the strongest barriers to post-secondary attendance, with gaps of 35 and 22 percentage points respectively. Gender and race/ethnicity are meaningful but secondary, and the race/ethnicity association is likely partially explained by overlap with economic disadvantage — particularly for American Indian students in the region.
High school characteristics contribute very little. District type has a negligible association with attendance, and while local unemployment and wage levels show statistically significant differences, the effect sizes are too small to be practically meaningful. Where a student goes to school matters far less than who that student is and what they do while they are there.
High school accomplishments tell the most differentiated story. PSEO participation is the single strongest predictor across all variables examined, followed closely by academic performance as measured by ACT scores and MCA proficiency in math, reading, and science. CTE engagement runs in the opposite direction — students with deeper CTE involvement are somewhat less likely to attend post-secondary — pointing to a distinct workforce-first orientation among that group that post-secondary attendance alone does not capture.
Taken together, these findings suggest that post-secondary attendance is shaped primarily by preparation and opportunity factors established well before graduation. Students who arrive at their senior year academically prepared, economically stable, and without a special education designation attend post-secondary at substantially higher rates. For students without those advantages, the gap in attendance is large and consistent across multiple measures.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics
All four demographic variables show a statistically significant relationship with post-secondary attendance, though effect sizes vary meaningfully across the group.
Special education status shows the strongest association (φ = 0.273). Students without a special education designation attended post-secondary at a rate of 73%, compared to 38% for students with a special education designation — a gap of 35 percentage points. The interpretation of this finding warrants some care, as post-secondary attendance may carry different meaning for special education students depending on individual transition plans and IEP goals.
Economic status is the second strongest predictor (φ = 0.228). Students not identified as economically disadvantaged attended post-secondary at 76%, compared to 54% for those who were — a 22-percentage-point gap. This association is likely intertwined with other demographic factors, particularly race/ethnicity, given the regional concentration of economically disadvantaged students among certain groups.
Race and ethnicity shows a statistically significant but more modest association (V = 0.164). White students had the highest post-secondary attendance rate at 72%, while American Indian students had the lowest at 52%. Other racial and ethnic groups clustered between 57% and 66%. A large “Unknown” category (n = 8,298) attended at 56%, and the non-random nature of that classification warrants caution in interpretation.
Gender shows the smallest effect in this group (φ = 0.121). Female graduates attended post-secondary at a rate of 74%, compared to 62% for male graduates — an 11-percentage-point gap that, while statistically significant, is modest relative to the other demographic predictors.
Taken together, special education status and economic status are the dominant demographic predictors of post-secondary attendance in this cohort. Gender and race/ethnicity are meaningful but secondary. The race/ethnicity association in particular should be interpreted alongside economic status, as overlap between these characteristics may account for a portion of the observed gap.
